## Paper

## Abstract

Surface plasmons are bound modes at metal–dielectric interfaces and enable a wide range of applications. However, holographic plasmonic fields are usually realized with complex nanostructures, introducing diffraction background and limiting flexibility and dynamic reconfigurability. Here, we propose a structureless holographic approach for generating complex plasmonic fields and controlling their energy flow through a reverse-designed algorithm. Both theoretical and experimental results demonstrate that holographic plasmonic fields can be effectively excited and flexibly modulated on a flat metal film. Furthermore, by loading orbital angular momentum onto the holographic plasmonic field, a controllable energy flow aligned with the plasmonic field can be achieved, visualizing through gold particles transporting along the designed trajectory like a surface slide. This work offers a promising structureless pathway for generation and manipulation of holographic plasmonic fields as well as other surface-wave fields, demonstrating significant potential for controllable on-chip optical energy and particle transmission.

---

## Introduction

Surface plasmons are electromagnetic eigenmodes bound to metal-dielectric interfaces, with evanescent fields that decay away from the surface1. By coupling incident light into these surface modes under appropriate wave-vector matching conditions, one obtains a propagating plasmonic wave that runs along the interface and remains tightly confined near it, effectively forming a near-field optical belt2–4. This confined plasmonic field possesses a shorter wavelength compared to the incident light, and enables the concentration of light into a deep subwavelength region through the storage of optical energy within electron oscillations. This phenomenon leads to a substantial enhancement of electromagnetic field at the nanoscale, thereby producing numerous valuable applications, such as plasmonic tweezers, plasmonic sensing, bioimaging, nano-lasers, and photonic circuits5–10. Consequently, the excitation of specifically designed plasmonic fields is essential to meet the diverse requirements of these applications.

The excitation of designed complex plasmonic fields typically necessitate the use of specialized metallic nanostructures11. Through the meticulous arrangement of nanostructures, holographic plasmonic fields with intricate spatial configurations can be generated12–19. For example, by spatially arranging nanostructures on a metallic film, it is feasible to generate specific structured holographic plasmonic fields12,20. To improve its adaptability, the configuration can be simplified to a single ring-shaped groove by merely customizing the excitation phase along the ring19. This approach facilitates the generation of diverse surface plasmonic modes through the excitation of a single nano-ring configuration. However, there are notable limitations associated with the excitation approach based on metallic nanostructures. Primarily, the metallic nanostructures introduce unavoidable diffraction components and significant energy losses, which detract from the fidelity of the generated plasmonic field20. Furthermore, the fixed nature of nanostructures imposes considerable constraints on the dynamic modulation of the excited plasmonic field. Additionally, most previous studies on holographic plasmonic fields have predominantly focused on holographic intensity distributions. Some other properties, such as energy flow, are challenging to manipulate according to desired patterns because the diffraction background perturbs the phase of the plasmonic field12,19–21. These properties are particularly important for the modulation of on-chip optical energy and particle transmission.

In this work, we propose a structureless and reverse-designed methodology aimed at generating desired complex plasmonic fields and controlling their energy flow. This methodology enables the creation and dynamic modulation of complex structured plasmonic fields on a flat metallic surface, eliminating the need for nanostructures. The strong correlation between theoretical and experimental results offers robust evidence for the feasibility of constructing and manipulating holographic plasmonic fields. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that by loading the ring-shaped orbital angular momentum (OAM) onto the incident light, the OAM can be transferred into the excited plasmonic field, resulting in a controllable unidirectional energy flow along the plasmonic field. To visualize the controllable energy flow within the holographic plasmonic fields, gold particles are employed to experimentally demonstrate the particle trapping by the plasmonic field and the particle transmission along the designed energy flow, akin to a surface slide. This research leverages the advantages of a structureless excitation methodology to manipulate holographic plasmonic intensity and energy flow fields, thereby offering a versatile on-chip optical manipulation platform applicable not only to surface plasmon but also to other optical surface waves such as Bloch surface wave22,23.

---

## Results

Principles
To generate a holographic plasmonic field, as illustrated in Fig. 1A, a specifically designed incident light field is utilized in a tight focusing system to illuminate a smooth metallic thin film. The high-NA focusing system provides large incident angles, so that the in-plane wave-vector components satisfy the required wave-vector matching condition for plasmon excitation5. In our approach, the incident light field is produced with a reversal design algorithm, which enables the precise control of the formed plasmonic field as desired. In this approach, the targeted holographic plasmonic field is expressed as a superposition of multiple plasmonic plane wave modes. By determining the expansion coefficients of each mode, which correspond to the initial plasmonic field distribution along an approximately ring-shaped excitation region that satisfies the wave vector matching conditions under tight focusing, the amplitude and phase of the incident light field are derived through the reversal design algorithm (See Methods Section). The amplitude and phase configuration of the reverse designed incident light field are then encoded onto a spatial light modulator (SLM), resulting in the generation of the targeted holographic plasmonic field.

To assess the efficacy of our methodology, experimental mapping for the generated plasmonic field was conducted in a metal nanoparticle-film system24 Moreover, to demonstrate the multifunctionality of the generated plasmonic field, OAM characterized by unidirectional phase gradients is integrated into the incident light field. The OAM is subsequently transferred into the plasmonic field, where the OAM induced energy flux along the plasmonic profile can drive the particles to move along a designed trajectory. Analogous to children’s slides Fig. 1B, the OAM within the surface plasmon field can generate surface slides, as illustrated in Fig. 1C. Detailed experimental configuration is presented in Fig. 1D and described in the Methods section.

Properties of the structureless excitation approach
To compare the performances of the structural and the structureless excitation approaches, Fig. 2 shows the FDTD results of an example of holographic plasmonic helix fields excited by two different methods, including the ring-shaped structural approach utilized in our previous work19 Fig. 2A and the structureless method Fig. 2D. The FDTD simulation methodologies are delineated in the subsequent Methods section and supplementary Note S1. In Fig. 2A, the nano-ring slit in Au film is essential for the excitation of the plasmonic field, thereby circumventing the strict excitation angle matching condition for incident light. The parameters of the ring structure are consistent with ref. 19, and the phase of the incident light is modified by the SLM to produce the helix plasmonic field. Fig. 2B presents the excited plasmonic helix field excited via the ring-shaped slit structure, with the yellow dashed line indicating the slit’s position. Although the predicted plasmonic field can be effectively excited, however, the fabricated ring-shaped slit strictly limit the position of excited plasmonic field within the ring structure, and brings the high requirement for incident beam alignment. Furthermore, the diffraction background induced by the structure significantly degrades the signal-to-noise ratio and accuracy of the generated plasmonic field. In addition, in the absence of the ring-shaped slit, the excitation efficiency of the plasmonic field becomes relatively low due to the rigorous wave-vector matching condition, resulting in a significantly weak and chaotic plasmonic field profile, as shown in Fig. 2C. In contrast, Fig. 2D, E illustrate the schematic and corresponding excited plasmonic helix field produced by our structureless method. The intensity and phase of the incident beam are derived through the proposed reversal design algorithm according to the predicted plasmonic helix field, as depicted in Fig. 2F (details see “Method” section). For a quantitative comparison, the amplitude distributions in Fig. 2B, E are calculated from electric fields that are normalized to an incident beam with an electric-field amplitude of 1 Vm⁻¹.

In the absence of structure-induced diffraction background, the pattern in Fig. 2E exhibits a significantly cleaner background and a higher excitation efficiency than that in Fig. 2B. Quantitatively, we define the coupling efficiency β as the ratio of the power coupled into the excited plasmonic field to the total input power (see supplementary Note S2 for the formal definition). With this definition, the coupling efficiency of our inverse-designed configuration reaches 18.5%, exceeding that of the ring-shaped structural approach (12.3%) by 6 percentage points, corresponding to a 50% relative improvement. Furthermore, it is important to highlight that this approach does not require the alignment between the incident beam and the ring slit, thereby providing great flexibility in shifting and re-shaping of the excited plasmonic field. As a result, with this structureless approach, desired holographic plasmonic patterns can be efficiently achieved with high modulation freedom and flexibility.

Calibration of the generated Plasmonic fields
To visualize and quantitatively assess the excited plasmonic field, a near-field nanoparticle scanning approach is employed to map the excited plasmonic fields25. Fig. 3 presents the comprehensive results of four examples of holographic plasmonic fields, namely Oval, Arc, Helix, and Cycloid, with typically non-centrosymmetric profiles (Corresponding phase distribution, see supplementary Note S3). Specifically, Fig. 3A shows the four targeted plasmonic field patterns (I0), characterized by a well-defined and sharp boundary, with the color depicting its spatial phase distribution. The phase undergoes periodic variations, resulting in a phase gradient along the plasmonic belt; consequently, akin to a plasmonic vortex26,27, it demonstrates OAM along its entire profile. Fig. 3B illustrates the theoretical distribution of the field (I1) excited by the incident field, as calculated using the reversal design algorithm. Due to the interference and diffraction effects, the background is not as clear as the targeted plasmonic field, with the presence of sidelobes. Fig. 3C presents the simulated results obtained by a FDTD solution (I2), verifying the correctness of the theoretical results Fig. 3B. According to the plasmonic field mapping through the near-field nanoparticle scanning approach, Fig. 3D presents the final experimental results (I3), indicating that the measured plasmonic intensity profiles exhibit a notable degree of similarity.

To quantitatively assess the degree of correlation between the pre-designated and the actually excited plasmonic fields, correlation indices of both the intensity and complex amplitude of the plasmonic fields are calculated (see Methods section and supplementary Note S4). The following Table 1 deliver the performances of the four representative fields in Fig. 3. Here, γ is the correlation index of field intensity and η is the correlation index of complex amplitude. To be consistent with the actual physical situations, correction indices of the FDTD simulations (I2) and experiments (I3) results are compared against the theoretical fields (I1). It is noted that only the intensity of the plasmonic field can be mapped in the experimental system; consequently, the index η for complex amplitude is lacking in this case.

The results in Table 1 indicate a strong degree of correspondence across all four scenarios, suggesting effective excitation of the pre-designated plasmonic fields in experiment. Notably, the case of cycloid-shaped plasmonic field performs a non-ideal match with a lower correlation index. This imperfect is mainly affected by the sharp corners of the field, which contains a significant amount of high-frequency spatial information. The spatial frequency of excited plasmonic field on gold film is subject to an upper limit, determined by the wave vector matching condition. Consequently, when addressing highly complex plasmonic field patterns, the required spatial frequency may exceed this limit, resulting in a deterioration of the observed effect.

Furthermore, Table 1 shows that the FDTD results are slightly degraded compared with the ideal theoretical values. This discrepancy mainly arises because the plasmonic field in theory is constructed as a superposition of plane waves, whose complex amplitude weights are prescribed by the inverse-design procedure. During the actual propagation of the plasmonic field, however, Joule losses and other dissipative mechanisms inevitably reshape these complex weights, leading to deviations between the simulated fields and the ideal target pattern, particularly in the high-frequency spatial components.

Particle transportation through plasmonic slide
It is well known that small objects within a plasmonic field experience plasmonic optical force, including both gradient and scattering components28. The gradient force arises from the spatial variation in the intensity of plasmonic field, resulting in the formation of a trapping potential well that attracts particles toward the high intensity region6. For example, Fig. 4A1 illustrates the trapping potential distribution of the Helix plasmonic field (simulation details see Method section and supplementary Note S5), which closely corresponds to its intensity profile depicted in Fig. 3. The scattering force, primarily resulting from the transfer of photon momentum from the light field to particles, is consistently directed along the Poynting vector (i.e, energy flux)18. As illustrated in Fig. 3A, OAM is included in the designed plasmonic fields, leading to a continuous energy flux along the plasmonic field profile, as indicated by the arrows in Fig. 4A2 being derived from FDTD simulations. The OAM-induced energy flux exerts a significant scattering force along the field profile, thereby enabling the dynamic actuation of particles. As a result, within the plasmonic field in a liquid environment, a particle is initially trapped at the plasmonic potential well by the gradient force, and then be transported by the scattering force along the energy flux of the field, acting like a slide for particles. Fig. 4A3 presents experimental results for particle manipulation, where the colored dots denote the motion trajectory of an Au particle (diameter of 0.8 μm) over time, demonstrating a high degree of consistency with the plasmonic field distribution.

Similarly, Fig. 4B–G display the energy flux of other three excited plasmonic fields in Fig. 3, along with the corresponding experimental manipulation results of the Au particles. Notably, the trajectories of trapped particles are highly consistent with the field intensity and energy flux distribution (see Supplementary Movie S1), demonstrating effectiveness of the proposed approach in particle transportation.

Ad libitum dynamic plasmonic slides
To further verify the diversity and dynamics of the proposed methodology, additional complex ad libitum plasmonic fields have been designed for particle manipulation. Fig. 5A shows the FDTD results of three designed plasmonic fields characterized by the letters S, Z, and U, with energy flux arrows along the field profiles. In experiment, gold nanoparticles are successfully trapped and guided along the trajectories of the letter S, Z, and U, as presented in Fig. 5B, further proving the reliability and diversity of our structureless holographic plasmonic technique (see Supplementary Movie S2).

Furthermore, due to the inherent advantages of a structureless design, excited plasmonic field can be dynamically adjusted by altering the incident holographic light field. By sequentially modulating a series of incident holograms, one can attain a time-averaged composite plasmonic field. The aforementioned analysis demonstrates that the two plasmonic fields can be easily produced, facilitating the independent trapping and movement of gold nanoparticles. Furthermore, the proposed structureless approach offers significant advantages in the dynamic manipulation of the excited plasmonic fields and the particle movement by simply altering the incident light field. Fig. 5C, D present the superimposed profiles of two distinct plasmonic fields generated successively in time, with their energy flux denoted by different colors. In Fig. 5C, two arc-shaped plasmonic fields are generated to form a heart-shaped field, enabling the guidance of particles along the heart-shaped profile through the successively activation of the two fields Fig. 5E (see Supplementary Movie S3).

Additionally, a specific nodal composite field with the ∞ configuration can also be generated with two S-shaped fields in different times, as illustrated in Fig. 5D. Correspondingly, Fig. 5F presents the final experimental manipulation tracks of the trapped gold particle, demonstrating a high degree of consistency with the predetermined design (see Supplementary Movie S4).

As a result, the navigation of particles along desired complex transmission pathways can be accomplished through the sequential excitation of multiple simple holographic plasmonic fields. This approach significantly improves the capacity for the on-chip transport of targeted microscopic objects.

In contrast to the widely-used structural excitation techniques for plasmonic fields, the proposed structureless approach offers several notable advantages. The structureless configuration demonstrates considerable dynamic benefits, such as the movable excitation position and the flexible profiles of the excited plasmonic fields. Furthermore, despite the stringent excitation conditions, the exciting efficiency remains relatively high and could be further enhanced when the incident light beam is shaped into a ring to perfectly match the surface plasmon resonant angle29. More importantly, the particle trapping process is highly repeatable and can be easily reestablished, thereby providing a stable and powerful tool for particle manipulation.

In particle trapping experiments, the incident laser inevitably introduces heating effect, which always brings thermal force and may cause damage on the trapped samples. To mitigate these adverse effects, a relatively low incident power of 5mW is utilized in experiments, significantly reduces thermodynamic impact compared to previous works30. It is essential to note that the thermal effect is not solely detrimental; previous researches have demonstrated that the plasmonic thermal effect can yield beneficial applications in special optical tweezers systems31, such as the thermoelectric and thermophoretic optical tweezers systems, and many other related technologies32–34. Thus, this approach represents an optimal strategy for plasmonic tweezers system, particularly in structureless configurations.

In addition to trapping metallic nanoparticles, our method is also applicable to the micromanipulation of dielectric particles (see Supplementary Note S6). To demonstrate its generality, we further perform trapping experiments with SiO₂ microspheres, showing that these dielectric particles can likewise be guided along trajectories prescribed by the holographic plasmonic fields. These results confirm the universality of our approach for microparticle trapping and transport.

---

## Methods

Reversal design algorithm
Similar to the beam shaping methodology utilized for generating free-space structured optical fields, here a reversal design algorithm is built for the generation of targeted plasmonic fields. The expression for any targeted plasmonic field can be derived as35:

E0(x,y) = 1/π ∫ exp[ik ∫ √(X'(θ)²+Y'(θ)²) dθ] exp[iΘ(x,y,θ)] dθ (1)

where, (x,y) represent the Cartesian coordinate system on the metallic surface where the targeted plasmonic field located, as shown in Fig. 6A; θ=atan(x/y) is the azimuthal coordinate on the metallic surface; Θ∈[−π,π] defines the integrating range of θ for the target plasmonic field; X(θ) and Y(θ) are the parametric functions that describe the two-dimensional trajectory of the targeted plasmonic field; X'(θ) and Y'(θ) are the derivatives of X(θ) and Y(θ), respectively; k is the wavenumber of plasmonic field, and w0 represents the beam waist. In Eq. 1, the initial exponential term denotes the Gaussian-decaying amplitude distribution of the plasmonic field, while the subsequent term illustrates the phase distribution along the field profile. For example, in Fig. 6A, X(θ)=−Sθcos(θ) and Y(θ)=−Sθsin(θ) describe a helix curve, with S is a real number that controls the size of the curve.

Since all initially excited plasmonic waves are focused towards the center to form the final plasmonic field on the metal surface, the desired holographic plasmonic field E0(x,y) can be treated as the superposition of plasmonic plane waves propagating in various directions. In accordance with the experimental scenarios, it is necessary to employ a discretization approximation of the azimuthal angle θ with a chosen step size of π=500. This step size offers a pragmatic balance between computational efficiency and the resolution of the plasmonic field. Accordingly, the targeted plasmonic field is expressed as a sum of plane waves:

E0(x,y) ≈ ∑ u(θ)ϕθ(x,y) = ∑ u(θ)exp[ikxsin(θ)] exp[ikycos(θ)] (2)

where E(x,y) represent the actual superimposed field of plane plasmonic waves on the metal surface; ϕθ(x,y) represent the plasmonic plane wave propagating with the azimuthal angle θ at the targeted plasmonic field location, and u(θ) is the complex amplitude function of the initially excited plasmonic plane wave. Therefore, the goal is to calculate u(θ), which can be expressed as:

u(θ) = 〈ϕθ(x,y)|E0(x,y)〉 (3)

where the symbol 〈·|·〉 represent the inner product of two fields, and the detailed simulation procedure is provided in Supplementary Note S7. From Eqs. (1–3), the amplitude and phase distribution of initial excited plasmonic plane waves at different angle θ can be calculated, as shown in Fig. 6B.

The above process explains how to use the targeted plasmonic field to reversal-calculate the initially excited plasmonic plane waves propagating in various directions. Since the above solution involves a discretization approximation, the final distribution of the focused plasmonic field exhibits a slight discrepancy with the designation. Furthermore, as the longitudinal component (Ez) shows an absolute predominance in the plasmonic field5, the above Eqs. 1 and 2 are adopted for the Ez component in a scalar format. Moreover, the Joule loss associated with plasmonic propagation is negligible, as the propagation distances of different plasmonic plane waves towards the center exhibit slight variations.

Distinct from conventional inverse-design techniques, such as Gerchberg–Saxton–type phase retrieval or adjoint-based gradient optimization, which typically require numerous iterations, rely on convergence checks, and are prone to local minima, our method avoids these issues, offers significantly higher computational efficiency, and retains a clear physical interpretation.

Design of the incident light field
To excite the initial plasmonic plane wave u(θ) above, an appropriate hologram can be designed and loaded onto the SLM. Since the amplitude of the initially excited plasmonic field is proportional to that of the excitation light field in free space36,37, the complex amplitude distribution of the light field in free space can be written as U(θ)=Cu(θ), where C is the plasmonic excitation coefficient. In this focusing system, to ensure that the incident light can be approximately perfectly matched to the plasmonic excitation angle29, consequently, the incident light field is designed as a ring-shaped field as shown in Fig. 6C. Accordingly, the incident light field is expressed as:

Ein = rect(r2−R1,R2) · Cu(θ), with (R2−R1) ≪ R2+R1 (4)

where, R1 and R2 represent the inner and outer radii of the ring (Fig. 6C), respectively; the rect(·) function represents the rectangular function, which describes an annular aperture with radius r∈[R1, R2] that covers the excitation angle.

To get the designed incident light field Ein, a holographic mask on SLM (Fig. 6C) that incorporates amplitude-phase modulation can be expressed as38:

Tmask = rect(r2−R1,R2) · |Cu(θ)| exp iangle[u(θ)] + 2πix/d (5)

where, |.| and angle(.) define the amplitude and phase angle of the field u(-θ). The term 2πix/d within the exponential function signifies a blazed grating with d is the grating period, which works in conjunction with the 4-f system. The light field diffracted by the mask, as shown in Fig. 6D, ultimately excites a plasmonic focus field on the metallic surface that closely matches the desired plasmonic field (Fig. 6A).

Calculation of correlation indices of the field
In order to quantitatively assess the quality of excited plasmonic field, it is important to calculate the correlation indices to the predetermined plasmonic field. Here, the mode purity coefficient index η, which indicates the correlation index of field complex amplitude, is defined as:

η = |〈E0(x,y)|Ej(x,y)〉|² (6)

where E0(x,y) and Ej(x,y) are complex amplitude of targeted and generated plasmonic fields, respectively. As a result, a value of 100% signifies that the two fields are exactly same in complex amplitude, whereas a value of 0% indicates that the two optical fields are entirely dissimilar.

The intensity distribution of plasmonic fields is also very important in various applications. Therefore, the intensity correlation index γ is evidently suitable for calibrating the efficacy of the generated plasmonic field, being defined as:

γ = |〈I0|Ij〉|² = |〈(E0(x,y))²|(Ej(x,y))²〉|² (7)

where, I and E are the intensity and complex amplitude of the plasmonic field, respectively. Experimental configuration
The structureless holographic plasmonic system is established on an inverted microscopic system (Olympus IX73), as schematically shown in Fig. 1D. In the configuration, a linearly polarized 532-nm laser beam (Changchun Leishi Photoelectric Technology Co., Ltd) initially passes through a polarizer (P) and a rotatable half-wave plate (HWP) to modulate the power. It is then expanded using a telescope system composed of two convex lenses (L1 and L2) to match the mask size of the hologram loaded on the SLM (PLUTO-2.1, 60Hz, HOLOEYE). A polarizer (P2) is employed to adjust the polarization orientation to align with the SLM. The incident polarized beam is then modulated by the holographic mask loaded on the SLM, which is achieved based on the reversal design algorithm. The encoded +1st-order diffraction from SLM is converted to radially polarized by a vortex plate (VP), and passes through a 4f-system (L3 and L4) to align with the back aperture of the oil-immersed objective lens (Olympus, 100×, NA=1.49). The encoded exciting light is then tightly focused onto a 35-nm thick gold film coated on the glass substrate to accommodate plasmonic field excitations. The gap between the objective lens and glass substrate is filled with oil, and a high-speed CMOS camera (Pointgrey, GS3-U3-23S6M-C) is used to capture the experimental process.

In this work, we perform two types of experiments: a field-mapping measurement to verify the generation of the holographic plasmonic field, and an optical-tweezing experiment to demonstrate its applicability to nanoparticle manipulation. Both experiments share the same optical setup; the main difference lies in the role of the nanoparticle. In the field-mapping experiment, the particle is immobilized on the metal film and used as a nanoscale probe that scatters the holographic plasmonic field for reconstructing its spatial distribution25. In the optical-tweezing experiment, the particle initially undergoes unrestricted motion within a liquid medium before being confined and manipulated by the holographic plasmonic field.

## Paper

## Abstract

Surface plasmons are bound modes at metal–dielectric interfaces and enable a wide range of applications. However, holographic plasmonic fields are usually realized with complex nanostructures, introducing diffraction background and limiting flexibility and dynamic reconfigurability. Here, we propose a structureless holographic approach for generating complex plasmonic fields and controlling their energy flow through a reverse-designed algorithm. Both theoretical and experimental results demonstrate that holographic plasmonic fields can be effectively excited and flexibly modulated on a flat metal film. Furthermore, by loading orbital angular momentum onto the holographic plasmonic field, a controllable energy flow aligned with the plasmonic field can be achieved, visualizing through gold particles transporting along the designed trajectory like a surface slide. This work offers a promising structureless pathway for generation and manipulation of holographic plasmonic fields as well as other surface-wave fields, demonstrating significant potential for controllable on-chip optical energy and particle transmission.

---

## Introduction

Surface plasmons are electromagnetic eigenmodes bound to metal-dielectric interfaces, with evanescent fields that decay away from the surface1. By coupling incident light into these surface modes under appropriate wave-vector matching conditions, one obtains a propagating plasmonic wave that runs along the interface and remains tightly confined near it, effectively forming a near-field optical belt2–4. This confined plasmonic field possesses a shorter wavelength compared to the incident light, and enables the concentration of light into a deep subwavelength region through the storage of optical energy within electron oscillations. This phenomenon leads to a substantial enhancement of electromagnetic field at the nanoscale, thereby producing numerous valuable applications, such as plasmonic tweezers, plasmonic sensing, bioimaging, nano-lasers, and photonic circuits5–10. Consequently, the excitation of specifically designed plasmonic fields is essential to meet the diverse requirements of these applications.

The excitation of designed complex plasmonic fields typically necessitate the use of specialized metallic nanostructures11. Through the meticulous arrangement of nanostructures, holographic plasmonic fields with intricate spatial configurations can be generated12–19. For example, by spatially arranging nanostructures on a metallic film, it is feasible to generate specific structured holographic plasmonic fields12,20. To improve its adaptability, the configuration can be simplified to a single ring-shaped groove by merely customizing the excitation phase along the ring19. This approach facilitates the generation of diverse surface plasmonic modes through the excitation of a single nano-ring configuration. However, there are notable limitations associated with the excitation approach based on metallic nanostructures. Primarily, the metallic nanostructures introduce unavoidable diffraction components and significant energy losses, which detract from the fidelity of the generated plasmonic field20. Furthermore, the fixed nature of nanostructures imposes considerable constraints on the dynamic modulation of the excited plasmonic field. Additionally, most previous studies on holographic plasmonic fields have predominantly focused on holographic intensity distributions. Some other properties, such as energy flow, are challenging to manipulate according to desired patterns because the diffraction background perturbs the phase of the plasmonic field12,19–21. These properties are particularly important for the modulation of on-chip optical energy and particle transmission.

In this work, we propose a structureless and reverse-designed methodology aimed at generating desired complex plasmonic fields and controlling their energy flow. This methodology enables the creation and dynamic modulation of complex structured plasmonic fields on a flat metallic surface, eliminating the need for nanostructures. The strong correlation between theoretical and experimental results offers robust evidence for the feasibility of constructing and manipulating holographic plasmonic fields. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that by loading the ring-shaped orbital angular momentum (OAM) onto the incident light, the OAM can be transferred into the excited plasmonic field, resulting in a controllable unidirectional energy flow along the plasmonic field. To visualize the controllable energy flow within the holographic plasmonic fields, gold particles are employed to experimentally demonstrate the particle trapping by the plasmonic field and the particle transmission along the designed energy flow, akin to a surface slide. This research leverages the advantages of a structureless excitation methodology to manipulate holographic plasmonic intensity and energy flow fields, thereby offering a versatile on-chip optical manipulation platform applicable not only to surface plasmon but also to other optical surface waves such as Bloch surface wave22,23.

---

## Results

Principles
To generate a holographic plasmonic field, as illustrated in Fig. 1A, a specifically designed incident light field is utilized in a tight focusing system to illuminate a smooth metallic thin film. The high-NA focusing system provides large incident angles, so that the in-plane wave-vector components satisfy the required wave-vector matching condition for plasmon excitation5. In our approach, the incident light field is produced with a reversal design algorithm, which enables the precise control of the formed plasmonic field as desired. In this approach, the targeted holographic plasmonic field is expressed as a superposition of multiple plasmonic plane wave modes. By determining the expansion coefficients of each mode, which correspond to the initial plasmonic field distribution along an approximately ring-shaped excitation region that satisfies the wave vector matching conditions under tight focusing, the amplitude and phase of the incident light field are derived through the reversal design algorithm (See Methods Section). The amplitude and phase configuration of the reverse designed incident light field are then encoded onto a spatial light modulator (SLM), resulting in the generation of the targeted holographic plasmonic field.

To assess the efficacy of our methodology, experimental mapping for the generated plasmonic field was conducted in a metal nanoparticle-film system24 Moreover, to demonstrate the multifunctionality of the generated plasmonic field, OAM characterized by unidirectional phase gradients is integrated into the incident light field. The OAM is subsequently transferred into the plasmonic field, where the OAM induced energy flux along the plasmonic profile can drive the particles to move along a designed trajectory. Analogous to children’s slides Fig. 1B, the OAM within the surface plasmon field can generate surface slides, as illustrated in Fig. 1C. Detailed experimental configuration is presented in Fig. 1D and described in the Methods section.

Properties of the structureless excitation approach
To compare the performances of the structural and the structureless excitation approaches, Fig. 2 shows the FDTD results of an example of holographic plasmonic helix fields excited by two different methods, including the ring-shaped structural approach utilized in our previous work19 Fig. 2A and the structureless method Fig. 2D. The FDTD simulation methodologies are delineated in the subsequent Methods section and supplementary Note S1. In Fig. 2A, the nano-ring slit in Au film is essential for the excitation of the plasmonic field, thereby circumventing the strict excitation angle matching condition for incident light. The parameters of the ring structure are consistent with ref. 19, and the phase of the incident light is modified by the SLM to produce the helix plasmonic field. Fig. 2B presents the excited plasmonic helix field excited via the ring-shaped slit structure, with the yellow dashed line indicating the slit’s position. Although the predicted plasmonic field can be effectively excited, however, the fabricated ring-shaped slit strictly limit the position of excited plasmonic field within the ring structure, and brings the high requirement for incident beam alignment. Furthermore, the diffraction background induced by the structure significantly degrades the signal-to-noise ratio and accuracy of the generated plasmonic field. In addition, in the absence of the ring-shaped slit, the excitation efficiency of the plasmonic field becomes relatively low due to the rigorous wave-vector matching condition, resulting in a significantly weak and chaotic plasmonic field profile, as shown in Fig. 2C. In contrast, Fig. 2D, E illustrate the schematic and corresponding excited plasmonic helix field produced by our structureless method. The intensity and phase of the incident beam are derived through the proposed reversal design algorithm according to the predicted plasmonic helix field, as depicted in Fig. 2F (details see “Method” section). For a quantitative comparison, the amplitude distributions in Fig. 2B, E are calculated from electric fields that are normalized to an incident beam with an electric-field amplitude of 1 Vm⁻¹.

In the absence of structure-induced diffraction background, the pattern in Fig. 2E exhibits a significantly cleaner background and a higher excitation efficiency than that in Fig. 2B. Quantitatively, we define the coupling efficiency β as the ratio of the power coupled into the excited plasmonic field to the total input power (see supplementary Note S2 for the formal definition). With this definition, the coupling efficiency of our inverse-designed configuration reaches 18.5%, exceeding that of the ring-shaped structural approach (12.3%) by 6 percentage points, corresponding to a 50% relative improvement. Furthermore, it is important to highlight that this approach does not require the alignment between the incident beam and the ring slit, thereby providing great flexibility in shifting and re-shaping of the excited plasmonic field. As a result, with this structureless approach, desired holographic plasmonic patterns can be efficiently achieved with high modulation freedom and flexibility.

Calibration of the generated Plasmonic fields
To visualize and quantitatively assess the excited plasmonic field, a near-field nanoparticle scanning approach is employed to map the excited plasmonic fields25. Fig. 3 presents the comprehensive results of four examples of holographic plasmonic fields, namely Oval, Arc, Helix, and Cycloid, with typically non-centrosymmetric profiles (Corresponding phase distribution, see supplementary Note S3). Specifically, Fig. 3A shows the four targeted plasmonic field patterns (I0), characterized by a well-defined and sharp boundary, with the color depicting its spatial phase distribution. The phase undergoes periodic variations, resulting in a phase gradient along the plasmonic belt; consequently, akin to a plasmonic vortex26,27, it demonstrates OAM along its entire profile. Fig. 3B illustrates the theoretical distribution of the field (I1) excited by the incident field, as calculated using the reversal design algorithm. Due to the interference and diffraction effects, the background is not as clear as the targeted plasmonic field, with the presence of sidelobes. Fig. 3C presents the simulated results obtained by a FDTD solution (I2), verifying the correctness of the theoretical results Fig. 3B. According to the plasmonic field mapping through the near-field nanoparticle scanning approach, Fig. 3D presents the final experimental results (I3), indicating that the measured plasmonic intensity profiles exhibit a notable degree of similarity.

To quantitatively assess the degree of correlation between the pre-designated and the actually excited plasmonic fields, correlation indices of both the intensity and complex amplitude of the plasmonic fields are calculated (see Methods section and supplementary Note S4). The following Table 1 deliver the performances of the four representative fields in Fig. 3. Here, γ is the correlation index of field intensity and η is the correlation index of complex amplitude. To be consistent with the actual physical situations, correction indices of the FDTD simulations (I2) and experiments (I3) results are compared against the theoretical fields (I1). It is noted that only the intensity of the plasmonic field can be mapped in the experimental system; consequently, the index η for complex amplitude is lacking in this case.

The results in Table 1 indicate a strong degree of correspondence across all four scenarios, suggesting effective excitation of the pre-designated plasmonic fields in experiment. Notably, the case of cycloid-shaped plasmonic field performs a non-ideal match with a lower correlation index. This imperfect is mainly affected by the sharp corners of the field, which contains a significant amount of high-frequency spatial information. The spatial frequency of excited plasmonic field on gold film is subject to an upper limit, determined by the wave vector matching condition. Consequently, when addressing highly complex plasmonic field patterns, the required spatial frequency may exceed this limit, resulting in a deterioration of the observed effect.

Furthermore, Table 1 shows that the FDTD results are slightly degraded compared with the ideal theoretical values. This discrepancy mainly arises because the plasmonic field in theory is constructed as a superposition of plane waves, whose complex amplitude weights are prescribed by the inverse-design procedure. During the actual propagation of the plasmonic field, however, Joule losses and other dissipative mechanisms inevitably reshape these complex weights, leading to deviations between the simulated fields and the ideal target pattern, particularly in the high-frequency spatial components.

Particle transportation through plasmonic slide
It is well known that small objects within a plasmonic field experience plasmonic optical force, including both gradient and scattering components28. The gradient force arises from the spatial variation in the intensity of plasmonic field, resulting in the formation of a trapping potential well that attracts particles toward the high intensity region6. For example, Fig. 4A1 illustrates the trapping potential distribution of the Helix plasmonic field (simulation details see Method section and supplementary Note S5), which closely corresponds to its intensity profile depicted in Fig. 3. The scattering force, primarily resulting from the transfer of photon momentum from the light field to particles, is consistently directed along the Poynting vector (i.e, energy flux)18. As illustrated in Fig. 3A, OAM is included in the designed plasmonic fields, leading to a continuous energy flux along the plasmonic field profile, as indicated by the arrows in Fig. 4A2 being derived from FDTD simulations. The OAM-induced energy flux exerts a significant scattering force along the field profile, thereby enabling the dynamic actuation of particles. As a result, within the plasmonic field in a liquid environment, a particle is initially trapped at the plasmonic potential well by the gradient force, and then be transported by the scattering force along the energy flux of the field, acting like a slide for particles. Fig. 4A3 presents experimental results for particle manipulation, where the colored dots denote the motion trajectory of an Au particle (diameter of 0.8 μm) over time, demonstrating a high degree of consistency with the plasmonic field distribution.

Similarly, Fig. 4B–G display the energy flux of other three excited plasmonic fields in Fig. 3, along with the corresponding experimental manipulation results of the Au particles. Notably, the trajectories of trapped particles are highly consistent with the field intensity and energy flux distribution (see Supplementary Movie S1), demonstrating effectiveness of the proposed approach in particle transportation.

Ad libitum dynamic plasmonic slides
To further verify the diversity and dynamics of the proposed methodology, additional complex ad libitum plasmonic fields have been designed for particle manipulation. Fig. 5A shows the FDTD results of three designed plasmonic fields characterized by the letters S, Z, and U, with energy flux arrows along the field profiles. In experiment, gold nanoparticles are successfully trapped and guided along the trajectories of the letter S, Z, and U, as presented in Fig. 5B, further proving the reliability and diversity of our structureless holographic plasmonic technique (see Supplementary Movie S2).

Furthermore, due to the inherent advantages of a structureless design, excited plasmonic field can be dynamically adjusted by altering the incident holographic light field. By sequentially modulating a series of incident holograms, one can attain a time-averaged composite plasmonic field. The aforementioned analysis demonstrates that the two plasmonic fields can be easily produced, facilitating the independent trapping and movement of gold nanoparticles. Furthermore, the proposed structureless approach offers significant advantages in the dynamic manipulation of the excited plasmonic fields and the particle movement by simply altering the incident light field. Fig. 5C, D present the superimposed profiles of two distinct plasmonic fields generated successively in time, with their energy flux denoted by different colors. In Fig. 5C, two arc-shaped plasmonic fields are generated to form a heart-shaped field, enabling the guidance of particles along the heart-shaped profile through the successively activation of the two fields Fig. 5E (see Supplementary Movie S3).

Additionally, a specific nodal composite field with the ∞ configuration can also be generated with two S-shaped fields in different times, as illustrated in Fig. 5D. Correspondingly, Fig. 5F presents the final experimental manipulation tracks of the trapped gold particle, demonstrating a high degree of consistency with the predetermined design (see Supplementary Movie S4).

As a result, the navigation of particles along desired complex transmission pathways can be accomplished through the sequential excitation of multiple simple holographic plasmonic fields. This approach significantly improves the capacity for the on-chip transport of targeted microscopic objects.

In contrast to the widely-used structural excitation techniques for plasmonic fields, the proposed structureless approach offers several notable advantages. The structureless configuration demonstrates considerable dynamic benefits, such as the movable excitation position and the flexible profiles of the excited plasmonic fields. Furthermore, despite the stringent excitation conditions, the exciting efficiency remains relatively high and could be further enhanced when the incident light beam is shaped into a ring to perfectly match the surface plasmon resonant angle29. More importantly, the particle trapping process is highly repeatable and can be easily reestablished, thereby providing a stable and powerful tool for particle manipulation.

In particle trapping experiments, the incident laser inevitably introduces heating effect, which always brings thermal force and may cause damage on the trapped samples. To mitigate these adverse effects, a relatively low incident power of 5mW is utilized in experiments, significantly reduces thermodynamic impact compared to previous works30. It is essential to note that the thermal effect is not solely detrimental; previous researches have demonstrated that the plasmonic thermal effect can yield beneficial applications in special optical tweezers systems31, such as the thermoelectric and thermophoretic optical tweezers systems, and many other related technologies32–34. Thus, this approach represents an optimal strategy for plasmonic tweezers system, particularly in structureless configurations.

In addition to trapping metallic nanoparticles, our method is also applicable to the micromanipulation of dielectric particles (see Supplementary Note S6). To demonstrate its generality, we further perform trapping experiments with SiO₂ microspheres, showing that these dielectric particles can likewise be guided along trajectories prescribed by the holographic plasmonic fields. These results confirm the universality of our approach for microparticle trapping and transport.

## Methods

Reversal design algorithm
Similar to the beam shaping methodology utilized for generating free-space structured optical fields, here a reversal design algorithm is built for the generation of targeted plasmonic fields. The expression for any targeted plasmonic field can be derived as35:

E0(x,y) = 1/π ∫ exp[ik ∫ √(X'(θ)²+Y'(θ)²) dθ] exp[iΘ(x,y,θ)] dθ (1)

where, (x,y) represent the Cartesian coordinate system on the metallic surface where the targeted plasmonic field located, as shown in Fig. 6A; θ=atan(x/y) is the azimuthal coordinate on the metallic surface; Θ∈[−π,π] defines the integrating range of θ for the target plasmonic field; X(θ) and Y(θ) are the parametric functions that describe the two-dimensional trajectory of the targeted plasmonic field; X'(θ) and Y'(θ) are the derivatives of X(θ) and Y(θ), respectively; k is the wavenumber of plasmonic field, and w0 represents the beam waist. In Eq. 1, the initial exponential term denotes the Gaussian-decaying amplitude distribution of the plasmonic field, while the subsequent term illustrates the phase distribution along the field profile. For example, in Fig. 6A, X(θ)=−Sθcos(θ) and Y(θ)=−Sθsin(θ) describe a helix curve, with S is a real number that controls the size of the curve.

Since all initially excited plasmonic waves are focused towards the center to form the final plasmonic field on the metal surface, the desired holographic plasmonic field E0(x,y) can be treated as the superposition of plasmonic plane waves propagating in various directions. In accordance with the experimental scenarios, it is necessary to employ a discretization approximation of the azimuthal angle θ with a chosen step size of π=500. This step size offers a pragmatic balance between computational efficiency and the resolution of the plasmonic field. Accordingly, the targeted plasmonic field is expressed as a sum of plane waves:

E0(x,y) ≈ ∑ u(θ)ϕθ(x,y) = ∑ u(θ)exp[ikxsin(θ)] exp[ikycos(θ)] (2)

where E(x,y) represent the actual superimposed field of plane plasmonic waves on the metal surface; ϕθ(x,y) represent the plasmonic plane wave propagating with the azimuthal angle θ at the targeted plasmonic field location, and u(θ) is the complex amplitude function of the initially excited plasmonic plane wave. Therefore, the goal is to calculate u(θ), which can be expressed as:

u(θ) = 〈ϕθ(x,y)|E0(x,y)〉 (3)

where the symbol 〈·|·〉 represent the inner product of two fields, and the detailed simulation procedure is provided in Supplementary Note S7. From Eqs. (1–3), the amplitude and phase distribution of initial excited plasmonic plane waves at different angle θ can be calculated, as shown in Fig. 6B.

The above process explains how to use the targeted plasmonic field to reversal-calculate the initially excited plasmonic plane waves propagating in various directions. Since the above solution involves a discretization approximation, the final distribution of the focused plasmonic field exhibits a slight discrepancy with the designation. Furthermore, as the longitudinal component (Ez) shows an absolute predominance in the plasmonic field5, the above Eqs. 1 and 2 are adopted for the Ez component in a scalar format. Moreover, the Joule loss associated with plasmonic propagation is negligible, as the propagation distances of different plasmonic plane waves towards the center exhibit slight variations.

Distinct from conventional inverse-design techniques, such as Gerchberg–Saxton–type phase retrieval or adjoint-based gradient optimization, which typically require numerous iterations, rely on convergence checks, and are prone to local minima, our method avoids these issues, offers significantly higher computational efficiency, and retains a clear physical interpretation.

Design of the incident light field
To excite the initial plasmonic plane wave u(θ) above, an appropriate hologram can be designed and loaded onto the SLM. Since the amplitude of the initially excited plasmonic field is proportional to that of the excitation light field in free space36,37, the complex amplitude distribution of the light field in free space can be written as U(θ)=Cu(θ), where C is the plasmonic excitation coefficient. In this focusing system, to ensure that the incident light can be approximately perfectly matched to the plasmonic excitation angle29, consequently, the incident light field is designed as a ring-shaped field as shown in Fig. 6C. Accordingly, the incident light field is expressed as:

Ein = rect(r2−R1,R2) · Cu(θ), with (R2−R1) ≪ R2+R1 (4)

where, R1 and R2 represent the inner and outer radii of the ring (Fig. 6C), respectively; the rect(·) function represents the rectangular function, which describes an annular aperture with radius r∈[R1, R2] that covers the excitation angle.

To get the designed incident light field Ein, a holographic mask on SLM (Fig. 6C) that incorporates amplitude-phase modulation can be expressed as38:

Tmask = rect(r2−R1,R2) · |Cu(θ)| exp iangle[u(θ)] + 2πix/d (5)

where, |.| and angle(.) define the amplitude and phase angle of the field u(-θ). The term 2πix/d within the exponential function signifies a blazed grating with d is the grating period, which works in conjunction with the 4-f system. The light field diffracted by the mask, as shown in Fig. 6D, ultimately excites a plasmonic focus field on the metallic surface that closely matches the desired plasmonic field (Fig. 6A).

Calculation of correlation indices of the field
In order to quantitatively assess the quality of excited plasmonic field, it is important to calculate the correlation indices to the predetermined plasmonic field. Here, the mode purity coefficient index η, which indicates the correlation index of field complex amplitude, is defined as:

η = |〈E0(x,y)|Ej(x,y)〉|² (6)

where E0(x,y) and Ej(x,y) are complex amplitude of targeted and generated plasmonic fields, respectively. As a result, a value of 100% signifies that the two fields are exactly same in complex amplitude, whereas a value of 0% indicates that the two optical fields are entirely dissimilar.

The intensity distribution of plasmonic fields is also very important in various applications. Therefore, the intensity correlation index γ is evidently suitable for calibrating the efficacy of the generated plasmonic field, being defined as:

γ = |〈I0|Ij〉|² = |〈(E0(x,y))²|(Ej(x,y))²〉|² (7)

where, I and E are the intensity and complex amplitude of the plasmonic field, respectively. Here, the mode purity index η is used to evaluate the shaping capability of the reversal design methodology applied to the plasmonic field, while the intensity correlation γ assesses the experimental outcomes.

Experimental configuration
The structureless holographic plasmonic system is established on an inverted microscopic system (Olympus IX73), as schematically shown in Fig. 1D. In the configuration, a linearly polarized 532-nm laser beam (Changchun Leishi Photoelectric Technology Co., Ltd) initially passes through a polarizer (P) and a rotatable half-wave plate (HWP) to modulate the power. It is then expanded using a telescope system composed of two convex lenses (L1 and L2) to match the mask size of the hologram loaded on the SLM (PLUTO-2.1, 60Hz, HOLOEYE). A polarizer (P2) is employed to adjust the polarization orientation to align with the SLM. The incident polarized beam is then modulated by the holographic mask loaded on the SLM, which is achieved based on the reversal design algorithm. The encoded +1st-order diffraction from SLM is converted to radially polarized by a vortex plate (VP), and passes through a 4f-system (L3 and L4) to align with the back aperture of the oil-immersed objective lens (Olympus, 100×, NA=1.49). The encoded exciting light is then tightly focused onto a 35-nm thick gold film coated on the glass substrate to accommodate plasmonic field excitations. The gap between the objective lens and glass substrate is filled with oil, and a high-speed CMOS camera (Pointgrey, GS3-U3-23S6M-C) is used to capture the experimental process.

In this work, we perform two types of experiments: a field-mapping measurement to verify the generation of the holographic plasmonic field, and an optical-tweezing experiment to demonstrate its applicability to nanoparticle manipulation. Both experiments share the same optical setup; the main difference lies in the role of the nanoparticle. In the field-mapping experiment, the particle is immobilized on the metal film and used as a nanoscale probe that scatters the holographic plasmonic field for reconstructing its spatial distribution25. In the optical-tweezing experiment, the particle initially undergoes unrestricted motion within a liquid medium before being confined and manipulated by the holographic plasmonic field.

Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the time and effort dedicated to evaluating
our manuscript and for acknowledging that the work is interesting, engaging, and
experimentally improves upon existing approaches. We appreciate the opportunity to
clarify the broader impact and fundamental importance of our contribution.
The conventional plasmonic manipulation approaches rely on nanostructures, which
inherently suffer from structural scattering, limited reconfigurability, and the inability
to control key properties such as energy flow. These limitations have long restricted the
fidelity and adaptability of plasmonic field engineering. In contrast, the present work
fundamentally addresses these challenges by introducing an unstructured, reverse-
engineered holographic excitation framework that enables an all-optical methodology.
This approach enables:
1. the generation of high-fidelity plasmonic fields devoid of structural scattering and
mode distortion;
2. real-time reconfigurability of plasmonic profiles integrated with optomechanical
functionality, representing a significant advancement toward scalable, and adaptive
plasmonic systems;
3.controllable energy flow driven by orbital angular momentum (OAM), capable of
transporting microparticles, thereby effectively realizing a structureless plasmonic
optical tweezers.
This nanofabrication-free and reprogrammable platform transcends the limitations of
static plasmonic configurations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first
demonstration of dynamically reconfigurable, structure-free holographic plasmonic
fields that support functional energy-flow manipulation. We believe that these
developments hold substantial potential for applications in precision manipulation, on-
chip sensing, and reconfigurable photonics.
Nevertheless, I have a couple of points that the authors can improve on, before
submitting the paper in a more specialized journal:
Comment 1: I'm a bit puzzled why the authors chose to do their experiments by

Reply 1: Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comments. We address your
questions point by point below.
(1) Why conduct experiments using optically trapped nanoparticles, instead of using a
probe tip for field mapping?
Optical manipulation at the nanoscale has become increasingly important as advanced
manufacturing, chip-level processing, and life sciences continue to progress toward
smaller length scales. Plasmonic optical tweezers are particularly attractive in this
context because the near-field confinement of surface plasmon polaritons enables
significantly stronger gradient forces and weaker scattering forces compared with
conventional free-space tweezers. However, this very advantage of plasmonic near
fields also imposes a fundamental limitation: their confinement to the metal surface
makes flexible modulation extremely challenging. Consequently, previous plasmonic
tweezers have only demonstrated relatively simple trapping and translation operations.
The central contribution of our work lies not only in the creation of a structureless
holographic plasmonic field, but also in demonstrating that such engineered fields can
substantially expand the manipulation capabilities of nanoparticles, enabling functions
that were previously inaccessible in plasmonic-field-based optical manipulation. The
use of gold nanoparticles highlights the capability of our method to achieve complex
and dynamic trapping in a highly challenging regime.
It is important to clarify that the field-mapping experiment is conceptually distinct from
the optical-tweezing experiment, and is specifically designed to verify that we indeed
generate the desired holographic plasmonic field. In the field-mapping measurements,
the gold nanoparticle is immobilized on the substrate and therefore does not undergo
Brownian motion. By analyzing the scattered field from this stationary nanoparticle,
we reconstruct the spatial distribution of the holographic plasmonic field, following the
procedure described in Ref. [25]. In contrast, in the optical-tweezing experiments, the
nanoparticles are freely trapped and transported by the engineered plasmonic field in a
liquid environment.
We fully agree that a probe-tip-based near-field method could also be used to measure
holographic plasmonic fields. Here, we chose not to adopt this approach primarily for
reasons of system compatibility and experimental simplicity. The stationary-
nanoparticle field-mapping method can be implemented within the same optical
platform as the plasmonic tweezers, without adding a separate near-field probe system.
This integration allows us to characterize and manipulate the holographic plasmonic
field in a unified setup, which is more practical and robust for the purposes of this work.
(2) Why not use dielectric particles for trapping?
Gold nanoparticles exhibit strong absorption and scattering, resulting in significant
scattering forces that make them difficult to trap using traditional free-space optical
tweezers. Therefore, demonstrating stable trapping of these challenging particles
provides clear validation of the enhanced capabilities offered by our holographic
plasmonic platform.
That said, our method is equally applicable to dielectric particles. To demonstrate this
generality, we have included experimental results using SiO₂ microspheres, which
exhibit stable trapping and guided transport along the designed holographic plasmonic
trajectory (see Fig. R4 and Supplementary Video). These results confirm that the
technique is robust for both metallic and dielectric particles.

Comment 2: I'm not sure how the authors match the momentum of the incident beam
with propagating SPP modes. From Fig.2, it seems that they always excite with normal
incidence. I understand in Fig2A that there is a nanoring slit that allows for this

Reply 2: Thank you for raising this important question. It is well known that the in-
plane momentum of an SPP exceeds that of light in free space, and therefore additional
momentum compensation is required for efficient excitation. Several common
wavevector-matching mechanism as follows.
The first configurations is prism-based coupling. The classical Otto and Kretschmann
configurations, introduced in 1968, compensate the in-plane momentum by tuning the
incidence angle(Fig. R5a-b) [Zeitschrift für Naturforschung A. 23, 2135-2136 (1968);
Zeitschrift für Physik A Hadrons and nuclei. 216, 398-410 (1968)]. This scheme is
simple and efficient, However, the propagating SPP diverge along the metal surface
and do not generate sufficiently strong optical gradient force, this approach has long
been considered unsuitable for optical trapping.
Second, surface plasmons can also be excited by near field scattering by a tip near a
metal surface (Fig. R5d), such as by particles or nanometre-sized scatters on a surface
(Fig. R5e). Since near-field scatterers have a wide spatial frequency spectrum, there are
components that will satisfy the matching conditions required to excite the SPP. This
approach is simple but often inefficient because only a small fraction of the scattered
light contributes to excitation. To enhance efficiency, periodic gratings are often
introduced. They supply defined spatial frequency components that mix with the
incident light and create strong momentum components matching the SPP wavevector
(Fig. R5f). The fixed nature of nanostructures greatly limits the dynamic modulation of
the excited plasmonic field. In addition, imperfections in the structures can introduce
extra scattering, leading to a reduction in the intensity of the desired optical field.
In our system, a high-NA objective produces a continuum of incident wavevectors
around the nominal optical axis (Fig. R5c). When the metal film is positioned
before the focal plane, only the annular portion of the illumination that meets the
surface-plasmon resonance (SPR) angle contributes to coupling. This annular
band functions similarly to the ring illumination used in prism-based schemes: it
selectively concentrates optical power near the required in-plane momentum while
suppressing direct transmission through the metal. The excited SPP then act as
secondary circular wave sources that propagate inward and coherently interfere to form
a strong central convergence point Ref. [5] & [Optics letters. 37,4627-4629 (2012)].
This coupling mechanism is directly responsible for the improved momentum matching
observed in Fig. 2D and subsequent configurations. The designed holographic
structures reshape the spatial phase of the incident field so that the high-NA objective
preferentially redistributes energy into the angular components that most efficiently
satisfy the SPP dispersion relation. As a result, this configuration inherently provides
the in-plane momentum required for efficient excitation of surface plasmons, while
eliminating fabrication-related constraints and maintaining high excitation efficiency.
[Plasmonics. 13, 991-996 (2018)]. Furthermore, this efficiency can be improved by
employing perfect radially polarized beams, by compressing the energy into a thin ring
that satisfies the plasmonic coupling conditions.[Photonics Research. 6, 847-852
(2018)].
